1.pericope_label: And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the Lord, she came to prove him with hard questions. And she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones: and when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart. And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not. And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house that he had built, And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the Lord; there was no more spirit in her. And she said to the king, It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard. Happy are thy men, happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and that hear thy wisdom. Blessed be the Lord thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the Lord loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice. And she gave the king an hundred and twenty talents of gold, and of spices very great store, and precious stones: there came no more such abundance of spices as these which the queen of Sheba gave to king Solomon.

schools.summary: Ellicott settles Sheba against Seba on a point of spelling the others miss, diagnoses the confusion of the two as the source of Josephus's queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, and infers from the kingdom being the Joktanite one that the queen was of Semitic race and not wholly alien from the stock of Abraham; Delitzsch denies that the hard questions had any religious character and corrects one item of the list from cupbearers to the drinking arrangements.
Gill reports the opinion of Josephus and rejects it without diagnosing it, places Sheba in the southern part of Arabia Felix, and collects the names given the queen in other traditions.

Clarke makes the hard questions riddles of the kind Eastern wisdom delighted in, charges the English version with having most pitifully departed from five other versions and from Luther over the ascent to the house of the Lord, and treats the failing of her spirit as a physical faint.

Henry records the Ethiopian claim but thinks Arabia the more probable, takes it that what she chiefly aimed at was instruction in the things of God, and turns her praise of Solomon into a charge on magistrates and ministers.

debates: Where Sheba was: Ellicott distinguishes it from Seba by the Hebrew letter and makes the queen Semitic, while Gill and Henry weigh the Ethiopian claim against Arabia.

What the hard questions were: riddles, problems and apologues of Eastern wisdom (Clarke), the enigmatic sayings in which Eastern philosophy embodied moral and religious speculation (Ellicott, with Henry going further), or simply sayings whose meaning was concealed, with no religious nature at all (Delitzsch).

Whether the fifth item of the list is the ascent Solomon made to the house of the Lord or the burnt offerings he offered there, where Clarke sets the Vulgate, Greek, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Luther against the English text.
outliers: Clarke supports the fainting from a case he saw himself, a lady who was an artist twice nearly overcome by exquisitely finished oriental paintings and obliged to leave the room.
Delitzsch reports that the earlier theologians inferred the queen's conversion to the true God from her blessing, taken together with our Lord's words about her.

11.pericope_label: And the navy also of Hiram, that brought gold from Ophir, brought in from Ophir great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones. And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the Lord, and for the king’s house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day. And king Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants.

schools.summary: Delitzsch clears three rival readings away from the almug work in turn, rejecting divans, panelled strips and moveables, and settles on steps with bannisters; Ellicott hears a position of inferiority in the terms of the parting gift, so that what she brought was of the nature of tribute, and explains the Eastern custom by which a thing is asked for by being praised.

Gill supplies the motive for the navy being mentioned here, that it shows Solomon had not all his gold from the queen but much from Hiram, puts Ophir in India with the classical authorities, and ties the almug work back to the ascent the queen had admired.

Clarke prefers the transposed spelling of the Chronicles parallel, works through five versions on the wood without deciding and takes the Arabic coloured wood for nearest the truth, and reports the tradition of a son born to Solomon by the queen.

debates: What the almug trees were: the thya or lignum vitae of the Vulgate, the pine of the Greek, the cypress of the Syriac, or the coloured wood of the Arabic that Clarke prefers.
What was made of the wood: steps with bannisters, as Delitzsch argues against three other readings, or the rails and supports of the causeway from the palace to the temple, as Gill has it.

What the parting gift amounted to: tribute rendered from a position of inferiority (Ellicott), the return presents Oriental custom obliged the king to make (Delitzsch), or, in the tradition Clarke reports, progeny.
outliers: Clarke passes on the tradition of the queen's own country that she bore Solomon a son named Menilek, who was brought up at the Israelite court, succeeded her, and introduced the Jewish religion among his subjects.

14.pericope_label: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred threescore and six talents of gold, Beside that he had of the merchantmen, and of the traffick of the spice merchants, and of all the kings of Arabia, and of the governors of the country. And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target. And he made three hundred shields of beaten gold; three pound of gold went to one shield: and the king put them in the house of the forest of Lebanon. Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the best gold. The throne had six steps, and the top of the throne was round behind: and there were stays on either side on the place of the seat, and two lions stood beside the stays. And twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps: there was not the like made in any kingdom. And all king Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of pure gold; none were of silver: it was nothing accounted of in the days of Solomon. For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.

schools.summary: Ellicott alone shows the standard he reckons the 666 talents by, prefers the silver standard and so the smaller figure, argues from the constant use of the word for foreign satraps that the governors are governors of tributary countries and that the word may be later than Solomon, and reads the throne ornament as Judah's lion and the twelve tribes with an Assyrian parallel that has horses where this has lions; Delitzsch prices the sum, guards it from two misreadings, and explains the shields and the ivory work technically.
Gill gives two valuations of the yearly revenue from other authorities and observes that the Carthaginians likewise made shields of gold.
Clarke reckons the yearly revenue at over four and a half million sterling.

Henry alone asks what the golden shields were for and answers that they were for state and not for service, reads the lions of the throne as a memorandum of the courage judgment requires, and is troubled that the same fleet that brought gold and ivory brought apes and peacocks.

debates: What the 666 talents come to: four commentators produce four figures, and only Ellicott states the talent he is reckoning by or explains why he prefers the lower sum.

Whether the sum can be read as strict annual taxation, which Delitzsch denies on two grounds, the Ophir fleet coming only once in three years and the revenue taking in commerce, domains and foreign presents.
Whether the governors of verse 15 are officers within Israel or governors of tributary countries, where Ellicott argues from the word's use of Syrian, Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian satraps.
outliers: Henry is the only witness who notices that the number of the talents is an ominous one and sends the reader to Revelation.

Ellicott meets the objection that the sum is incredible by pointing to the Mexicans and Peruvians before the Spanish conquests, among whom gold was abundant enough to pass out of currency into ornament.

23.pericope_label: So king Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom. And all the earth sought to Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart. And they brought every man his present, vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and garments, and armour, and spices, horses, and mules, a rate year by year. And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he bestowed in the cities for chariots, and with the king at Jerusalem. And the king made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance. And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt, and linen yarn: the king’s merchants received the linen yarn at a price. And a chariot came up and went out of Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty: and so for all the kings of the Hittites, and for the kings of Syria, did they bring them out by their means.

schools.summary: Delitzsch rests the summary on a tense, that Solomon became and not was the greatest of kings, reads the list of presents plainly, and refuses to divide the price of a chariot by the price of a horse to get the size of the team, since the car itself would not have been given in; Ellicott asks what the chariots are doing in a chapter about commerce and answers that they held the kingdom together, turns the silver made common as stones into a political observation about a capital enriched while the provinces were oppressed, prefers the Septuagint reading from Tekoa, and confirms the Hittite kings from Egyptian and Assyrian inscriptions.
Gill calls the silver a hyperbolical expression, observes only that the horses out of Egypt seem contrary to the command, and converts the shekel prices while correcting his own rate as he goes.

Clarke says outright that God had absolutely prohibited horses and that in many things Solomon paid little attention to the divine command, lays out five attempts on the word rendered linen yarn and prefers Bochart's as the text stands while granting Houbigant's makes the best sense, and takes the Hittite kings for a Canaanite remnant gone north into a principality.

Henry refuses to admire the greatness, recalling that the man who exceeded all the kings of the earth had asked at the outset for an understanding heart and afterwards wrote a whole book to show the vanity of what he had gained.

debates: What the word rendered linen yarn means: a place name (the Vulgate and the Septuagint, with Ellicott preferring Tekoa), the tribute farmed at a price (Bochart, whom Clarke follows), the cord tying one horse to another, a drove or stud (Jarchi), or a corruption of the word for chariots (Houbigant).

Whether silver made common as stones is abundance or loss: Gill and Delitzsch read it as hyperbole for plenty, Clarke as the destruction of silver's value, and Ellicott as wealth gathered into Jerusalem and the court while the general population was left impoverished.
Whether the price of a chariot yields the number of horses in its team, which Delitzsch denies against both the four-horse reading and the reading of two draught horses with two in reserve.
outliers: Ellicott notes that horses are not represented on Egyptian monuments before the eighteenth dynasty, although Egypt abounded in them, and suggests they were introduced by the Hyksos.
